job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run my days like a project. Up at seven, a run round the reservoir, then two hours on applications using a spreadsheet where I track every firm, date and follow-up. Then I do a coding exercise or a bit of a machine learning course, and in the afternoon I tutor two teenagers online in maths. I rent a room in a house in Dalton Green with three others, and we cook together on Thursdays, which is the highlight of the week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me what you studied and how the search is going.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer science with a data focus and finished in June with a good result. My final project was a tool that sends appointment reminders for a hospital clinic and predicts who'll miss a slot. I spent ten weeks at an insurance company, Marlowe Mutual, on their claims data team. Since then I've sent about a hundred applications, got five interviews and no offers. I'm carrying heavy student debt, I've got maybe two weeks of living costs saved, and my family can't help, since my mum's a care worker and Dad's retired early with a bad back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say okay, that's a relief, and then I'd say the market is still hard. I'd tell friends to ignore both the doom and the hype and just do the work. I'd also say that employers should stop asking for three years of experience for a graduate job, because it's a bit silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little. I'd still be one of a few hundred applicants for each data job, and I'd still be sitting on two weeks of money. AI saves me a bit of time with code and writing, so I'd be a little faster, but so would everyone else. I'd say the market is flat and that makes me anxious, not calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the spreadsheet and tune it. I'd go back to the five firms that interviewed me and ask for feedback, because that's information I can use. I'd apply to smaller companies and public bodies, not only big names. I'd take on more tutoring, maybe six students instead of two. And I'd keep using AI to speed up applications and practice coding problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady on top and shaky underneath. I'm good at looking calm, and then at three in the morning I'm doing the arithmetic on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your spreadsheet tell you about which firms respond?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller firms and public bodies respond more, and big ones ghost me. Four of my five interviews were with firms under two hundred people. Referrals from people I've met at meetups get an answer within a day, and the cold applications get an answer in a month, if ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money come from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tutoring, a hundred and forty pounds a month, and my housemates' patience. I'm not proud of the second one. My rent's paid up to the end of the month, and after that I'd have to borrow from my sister Nora, who has a baby and no spare cash.

say: I'd tell friends to ignore both doom and **hype** and just do the work.
Employers should stop asking for three years of experience for a graduate job.
think: Very little changes: still a few hundred applicants for each data job, and **two weeks** of money.
AI makes me a bit faster, but it does so for everyone.
do: Ask the five firms that interviewed me for **feedback**.
Apply to smaller companies and public bodies, not only big names.
Take on six tutoring students instead of two.
feel: Doing the rent arithmetic at three in the morning.
S0.quote: Referrals from people I've met at meetups get an answer within a day, and the cold applications get an answer in a month, if ever.
fieldNote: She treats the search as **data**, tracking firms and response times.
Money is the real pressure, with her sister Nora as the last cushion she does not want to use.
Her calm is a **performance** that she admits slips at night.

steps.text: Ask the five firms that interviewed me for feedback
Apply to smaller firms and public bodies in the region
Take on six online tutoring students instead of two
Use AI to speed up applications and coding practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should get on with learning the tools. I'd tell friends that being the person who can use AI well and check its answers is the job now. I'd also say that universities should be teaching this, and firms should be training people to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's two-sided. It makes my kind of entry job smaller, cleaning data, running reports, writing summaries, checking numbers, because those are tasks software does. But I'm comfortable with the tools, so I can pitch myself as someone who can do the work of two. The problem is that firms hire fewer juniors, so I'm competing with other people just as ready as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a portfolio with two or three projects that use real data, like my appointment tool, and show how I checked the model's output. I'd pitch small firms that can't afford a data team, offering a short paid project. And I'd learn about data protection and risk, because someone has to be accountable for what the models do. Firms like Marlowe Mutual need that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up, if I'm honest, but with a thread of fear. It's like the start of a race with a lot of strong runners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a data analyst's first year does software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cleaning and the reporting. At Marlowe I spent three weeks on a data cleaning task that I'd now finish in an afternoon with a good tool. The firm didn't need me for three weeks, it needed me for the judgement call about what counted as an error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if every junior role asked you to manage AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes happily, but I'd want to learn to say when the AI is wrong. That's the skill I think will be worth money. So I'd treat the job as supervising a very fast, very confident junior who sometimes lies.

say: I'd say being the person who can use AI well and **check** its answers is the job now.
Universities and firms should be teaching this.
think: It shrinks entry jobs like data cleaning and reports, but I can **pitch** myself as doing the work of two.
Fewer junior roles mean competing with equally ready people.
do: Build a portfolio of two or three **real-data** projects showing how I checked the output.
Pitch small firms a short paid project, since they can't afford a data team.
feel: **Fired up**, with a thread of fear.
Like the start of a race with strong runners.
S1.quote: I'd treat the job as supervising a very fast, very confident junior who sometimes lies.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **colleague to supervise**, and it shapes her pitch to small firms.
The Marlowe cleaning story gives a concrete example of tasks that vanish.
Her edge is **judgement**, and she knows it must be shown, not claimed.

steps.text: Build two portfolio projects showing how I checked the model output
Pitch small firms a short paid data project
Take a short course on data protection and risk
Apply for data analyst roles at small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big thing is, don't pretend. Companies and governments need to say what they'll do, loudly and soon. I'd say it's a time for sharing, paid training, income support, and rules to slow things down. Online I'd write long, calm posts about it, because shouting won't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my fear is that my field is exactly the one they mean. Data, coding, reports and analysis are all thinking work, so there's no three-year grace period for me, it arrives on the date. In two years I'd be a graduate with a loan and no experience competing against a machine that never sleeps. I don't see how it ends well for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any job at all now, anything with a pay slip, and I'd quit paying for courses. I'd look at care and health support, since my mum works in care and I know how short of people the sector is, and humans there matter. I'd save every pound and tell my housemates early that I might have to leave. And I'd use AI tools to do whatever freelance tasks I can quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. I check the tracker spreadsheet and the whole sheet looks pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plan in the first month after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My plan collapses and I rebuild it from scratch. The spreadsheet gets thrown out. I'd focus on only three numbers: money in, money out and weeks until it's gone. Then I'd call my sister Nora and my mum, and I'd ask what they can do, and what they can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be hit hardest in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably. She's a care worker and fine for now, but she's the only one earning in our family and she works nights. If something changed in care, all of us would be exposed. I think about that more than about myself.

I'd write long, calm posts, because shouting won't help.
think: My field is exactly the one they mean, so there's no **grace period** for me.

Look at care and health support, where humans still matter.
Tell my housemates early that I might have to leave.
feel: **Dizzy**, with my tracker sheet suddenly looking pointless.

S2.quote: I'd focus on only three numbers: money in, money out and weeks until it's gone.
fieldNote: Her **method** breaks down but then compresses to three numbers, which shows resilience.
She thinks of her mum, the only earner, before herself, and that is the **real fear**.
Care work is a lateral move she knows from home.

steps.text: Take any job that gives a pay slip

Look into care and health support roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan and short enough to take seriously. I'd say it online and to my friends. I'd tell people to build a financial cushion, learn the tools and keep asking their employers what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better than two years, though not comfortable. I can get a first job, probably a data or analyst role, and then build experience while the clock runs. I'd have maybe three years inside a firm before the thinking jobs are replaced, which makes me a person who knows how the place works. That has to be worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent entry role, even a bit below what I wanted, and learn everything I could, especially the business side. I'd save a third of my pay, pay the loan faster, and in year two decide between going deeper in AI safety and data governance, or moving into health or care services. I'd keep tutoring because teaching is something I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, more like a puzzle than a cliff. I'm still jumpy about the loan, but I can make a plan and the plan feels real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend the first of those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year, I'd get a job, any job. I'd treat it like a foundation: get the rent covered, find a mentor, learn how the firm runs. And I'd finish the part of the loan that costs the most in interest, so the clock isn't running against me in two directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cousin about choosing a degree now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to do something she's curious about but pair it with a practical skill. Don't pick purely because the pay is good right now. Learn to work with people. Learn how organisations actually run. A degree that makes you adaptable matters more than one that makes you specialised.

Build a financial cushion and keep asking employers what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we have time, so let's not waste it. I'd tell people to use the next few years to build skills that mix tech with people, and I'd push for employers to share what they plan. I'd say it's a decade to get the rules right, not to sit back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay, even a bit excited. A decade is enough to build a career, move through two roles and maybe run a small team before it all shifts. I'd still be only thirty-three, and I'd be one of the people who understands how these systems work from the inside. That has to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, pay the loan down fast, and try to move into a role that mixes data with people, like health analytics or clinic operations, where I can use my appointment tool experience. I'd save for a deposit and take a short course every year. And I'd mentor graduates a few years behind me, because I know how hard this was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some fizz. It feels like standing at the start of a long road with decent shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what's the biggest bet you'd make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bet on health. My hospital tool showed me that clinics lose real money and real patients when people miss appointments, and that work is part data and part people. If I could build my career around that, I'd feel useful and I'd be harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your family to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm going to be fine and that they don't have to worry about me. And then I'd want to help them, a bit at a time. I'd want Mum to cut her night shifts and Dad to see a proper specialist for his back. That's the point of this whole decade for me.

say: I'd say it's a decade to get the rules **right**, not to sit back.
Employers should share what they plan.
think: A decade is enough to build a **career**, move through two roles and understand these systems from inside.

Save for a deposit and take a short course every year.
Mentor graduates a few years behind me.

fieldNote: She picks **health** analytics because her own project showed her a real problem there.
Her wish to help her parents is clear and is what she wants the decade for.
She stays **anxious**, as debt and a thin first-job market still decide her next two years.

steps.text: Pay the student loan down fast after the first job
Move toward health analytics or clinic operations
Take one short course every year
Save for a flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no contest. It leaves no grace period, because my work is the work they say goes first. What would help is dull and practical: graduate jobs that actually exist, a way to pause loan payments when there's no income, and honest information early so I can plan. I'd love it if firms hired for potential and trained people, instead of asking for experience nobody can get.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as calm as I sound. I run my life with spreadsheets because it keeps panic away. If people reading this are in a similar spot, I'd want them to know this. Being organised isn't the same as being okay, and it's fine to ask for help.

headlineQuote: Being organised isn't the same as being okay, and it's fine to ask for help.
portrait: Esther is a **23-year-old** computer science graduate in a shared house, with a hundred applications, five interviews and no offer yet.
She built a hospital reminder tool, and has heavy debt, two weeks saved and **no family** money.
She is a pragmatic centrist who uses AI every day, tracks her search in a spreadsheet and supervises tools as a skill.
Adaptive and risk-tolerant, she plans in **sequence**, moving toward health analytics, governance or care.
She is anxious in most pictures, alarmed with two years, and still anxious with ten because debt sets the pace.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most, because her own thinking work goes first and gives no grace period.
whatWouldHelp: Real **graduate jobs**, paused loan payments when income stops, and honest early information from firms and governments.
